---
title: "Parameter recovery"
---

A model may fit without warnings even when the observed design contains too little information to separate its quantities. **Parameter recovery** tests the complete inference procedure on simulated responses whose generating values are known. Here the simulation preserves the exact item--annotator incidence pattern of the UDS natural-parts extract introduced on the [first page](generative-stories.qmd).

We generate synthetic responses from the proposed model on the observed
item--annotator incidence graph and then refit the complete procedure. Recovery of
the known generating quantities checks computation and the information supplied by
that design, conditional on the generator. Evidence that real annotations follow
the generator must instead come from the measurement argument and
[posterior predictive checks](../statistical-inference/posterior-predictive-checks.qmd),
which compare observed response summaries with the same summaries computed from
response tables generated under posterior draws. The rows, identities, and imbalance
come from the released annotation design; the generating values and acceptance
criteria were fixed before the released responses were fit.

We state the complete generator and Stan model, then evaluate whether repeated fits
recover the known population and group-level quantities under the released design.

## The released design and recovery runs {#loading-released-design-and-completed-fits}

```{r}
#| label: load-uds-recovery
#| message: false
#| warning: false

uds <- utils::read.csv(
  "data/uds/uds-natural-parts.csv",
  check.names = FALSE
)
cache_path <- "data/uds/uds-natural-parts-posterior-cache.rds"
uds_cache <- readRDS(cache_path)

stopifnot(
  nrow(uds) == 2955L,
  length(unique(uds$item_id)) == 1000L,
  length(unique(uds$annotator_id)) == 12L,
  nrow(uds_cache$recovery) == 12L,
  nrow(uds_cache$population_draws) == 400L,
  ncol(uds_cache$item_effect_draws) == 1000L,
  ncol(uds_cache$annotator_effect_draws) == 12L,
  identical(uds_cache$item_levels, unique(uds$item_id)),
  identical(uds_cache$annotator_levels, unique(uds$annotator_id)),
  identical(
    digest::digest(file = cache_path, algo = "sha256"),
    "19b9920f55506717d9b54667f9495f9703d6e5fc213b5f4fb4350f99096bfb08"
  ),
  identical(
    unname(uds_cache$provenance$source_csv_sha256),
    "a9d49305fe6b4780a0f3da845bd3d6bc8ed8908c3664c6931180d4346a46e2f8"
  ),
  identical(
    unname(uds_cache$provenance$source_fit_sha256),
    "f48a5b9d37fc91728804366515b8c34864fa69f9ece7755f33a6007a4641005c"
  ),
  identical(
    unname(uds_cache$provenance$stan_sha256),
    "5d85750a5090c6b1cd709844336372e945ec85e68f8391f0c72d7a8141329fc0"
  ),
  identical(uds_cache$provenance$fit_seeds, 880001:880004),
  identical(
    uds_cache$provenance$retained_cache_rows,
    seq(4L, 3200L, by = 8L)
  )
)

uds$item_index <- match(uds$item_id, uds_cache$item_levels)
uds$annotator_index <- match(
  uds$annotator_id,
  uds_cache$annotator_levels
)

recovery <- uds_cache$recovery
generating_values <- c(
  alpha = -2.1, # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  sigma_item = 1.6, # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  sigma_annotator = 1.6 # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
)

stopifnot(
  all(abs(
    recovery$alpha_estimate - recovery$alpha_error -
      generating_values[["alpha"]]
  ) < 1e-10),
  all(abs(
    recovery$sigma_item_estimate /
      (1 + recovery$sigma_item_relative_error) -
      generating_values[["sigma_item"]]
  ) < 1e-10),
  all(abs(
    recovery$sigma_annotator_estimate /
      (1 + recovery$sigma_annotator_relative_error) -
      generating_values[["sigma_annotator"]]
  ) < 1e-10)
)
```

The analysis contains `r nrow(uds_cache$recovery)` complete recovery replicates. In
each one, responses are generated from known population and group quantities and the
same model is fit back to those responses. We can therefore compare each posterior
summary with the value that generated its data.

## The complete Stan program

The crossed response model uses a **non-centered parameterization**. Rather than
sampling each deviation $u_i$ directly on a scale set by an unknown $\sigma$, we
sample a standard-normal coordinate $z_i$ and construct $u_i=\sigma z_i$. The two
forms describe the same conditional distribution, but their sampling coordinates
can have different posterior dependence; the
[divergence page](../statistical-inference/divergent-transitions.qmd) develops this
computational motivation. Here we also center the realized standard-normal vectors,
which fixes the finite-sample sums of the resulting item and annotator deviations at
zero.

```{r}
#| label: define-uds-stan-program
#| eval: false

stan_program <- '
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> I;
  int<lower=1> A;
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=I> item;
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=A> annotator;
  array[N] int<lower=0, upper=1> response;
}

parameters {
  real alpha;
  real<lower=0> sigma_item;
  real<lower=0> sigma_annotator;
  vector[I] z_item_raw;
  vector[A] z_annotator_raw;
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[I] z_item = z_item_raw - mean(z_item_raw);
  vector[A] z_annotator = z_annotator_raw - mean(z_annotator_raw);
  vector[I] item_effect = sigma_item * z_item;
  vector[A] annotator_effect = sigma_annotator * z_annotator;
}

model {
  alpha ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  sigma_item ~ normal(0, 2);
  sigma_annotator ~ normal(0, 2);
  z_item_raw ~ std_normal();
  z_annotator_raw ~ std_normal();

  response ~ bernoulli_logit(
    alpha + item_effect[item] + annotator_effect[annotator]
  );
}
'
```

The priors provide **regularization** by combining the sparse evidence for each
group-specific deviation with a shared population distribution. Weakly informed
deviations are consequently pulled toward the population center, much as the
penalty in [ridge regression](../regression-models/ridge-regression.qmd) pulls weakly
supported coefficients toward zero. Here `normal(0, 2.5)` places the population log
odds near no directional preference while allowing a wide range of gate
probabilities. Because the two scale parameters are constrained positive,
`normal(0, 2)` becomes a half-normal prior: it favors smaller heterogeneity while
retaining substantial positive mass. The standard-normal raw deviations implement
the non-centered parameterization defined above, which often reduces posterior
dependence between group effects and their scales. These weakly regularizing choices
are assumptions we make before fitting, rather than facts learned from the response
table; the [full measurement model](uds-measurement-model.qmd#writing-the-complete-model)
checks their implications with prior and posterior prediction.

## The exact recovery generator and fitting call

The code below is the executable core of one replicate. It uses the observed row
indices without changing which annotator saw which item. We ran replicates 1 through
12; simulation seed $7300+s$ generated replicate $s$, and the two fitting chains
used seeds $740000+100s+c$ for chain $c$.

```{r}
#| label: recovery-generator-and-fit
#| eval: false

model <- cmdstanr::cmdstan_model(
  cmdstanr::write_stan_file(stan_program)
)

recover_one <- function(replicate, generating_values) {
  set.seed(7300L + replicate)

  z_item <- stats::rnorm(length(uds_cache$item_levels))
  z_item <- z_item - mean(z_item)
  z_annotator <- stats::rnorm(length(uds_cache$annotator_levels))
  z_annotator <- z_annotator - mean(z_annotator)

  true_item_effect <- generating_values[["sigma_item"]] * z_item
  true_annotator_effect <-
    generating_values[["sigma_annotator"]] * z_annotator
  eta <-
    generating_values[["alpha"]] +
    true_item_effect[uds$item_index] +
    true_annotator_effect[uds$annotator_index]

  simulated_response <- stats::rbinom(
    nrow(uds),
    size = 1,
    prob = stats::plogis(eta)
  )

  stan_data <- list(
    N = nrow(uds),
    I = length(uds_cache$item_levels),
    A = length(uds_cache$annotator_levels),
    item = uds$item_index,
    annotator = uds$annotator_index,
    response = simulated_response
  )

  lapply(seq_len(2L), function(chain) {
    model$sample(
      data = stan_data,
      chains = 1,
      parallel_chains = 1,
      chain_ids = chain,
      iter_warmup = 400,
      iter_sampling = 400,
      seed = 740000L + 100L * replicate + chain,
      adapt_delta = 0.95,
      refresh = 0
    )
  })
}

recovery_fits <- lapply(
  seq_len(12L),
  recover_one,
  generating_values = generating_values
)
```

Two chains with 400 warmup and 400 retained draws made twelve complete fits feasible
while still permitting an $\widehat R$ comparison. This design provides less
between-chain information and smaller
[effective sample sizes](../statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd) than the
four or more chains appropriate for a final high-dimensional fit. `adapt_delta =
0.95` asks Stan for smaller integration steps than its default and was chosen to
reduce divergent transitions in the hierarchical geometry. It can improve numerical
exploration, but it cannot identify a weakly informed parameter.

Only the baseline generating regime was simulated and fit. A stronger recovery
analysis should cross the observed incidence design with at least three additional
conditions fixed before inspecting the results:

| Regime | $\alpha$ | $\sigma_{\mathrm{item}}$ | $\sigma_{\mathrm{annotator}}$ | Stress being tested |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Baseline | -2.1 | 1.6 | 1.6 | evaluated here | <!-- dqr-allow: algorithm-setting -->
| Weak heterogeneity | -2.1 | 0.5 | 0.5 | separation of scales near zero | <!-- dqr-allow: algorithm-setting -->
| Rarer yes responses | -3.2 | 1.6 | 1.6 | information under a lower event rate | <!-- dqr-allow: algorithm-setting -->
| Strong annotator spread | -2.1 | 1.6 | 2.4 | separation under dominant annotator variation | <!-- dqr-allow: algorithm-setting -->

The revised `recover_one()` accepts the generating vector as an argument, so those regimes can use the same fitting code and incidence design. Their rows state planned stress tests; numerical results are available only for the twelve completed baseline fits.

## Evaluating parameter recovery

For replicate $s$, an error is $\widehat\theta_s-\theta_s$. Across $S$ replicates, estimated bias and root mean squared error are

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Bias}}
=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S(\widehat\theta_s-\theta_s),
$$

$$
\operatorname{RMSE}
=\sqrt{\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S
(\widehat\theta_s-\theta_s)^2}.
$$

For a positive scale, the relative error used below is

$$
e^{\mathrm{rel}}_s
=\frac{\widehat\sigma_s-\sigma}{\sigma}
=\frac{\widehat\sigma_s}{\sigma}-1.
$$

Dividing by the generating scale makes item and annotator scale errors comparable,
though it becomes unstable when the truth approaches zero. A
[correlation](../random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd) standardizes
covariance. The latent-effect correlations compare the generated and
posterior-median vectors after their zero-sum coordinate constraint. They measure
recovery of ordering and relative spacing, not equality of every effect. The
item-probability correlation asks the same ordering question after the nonlinear
inverse-logit map.

We use medians and recovery correlations because the target includes population
scales and high-dimensional latent orderings. We call the cutoffs fixed before
fitting the **recovery acceptance criteria for this analysis**. They are decision
rules tied to the later use of these quantities: intercept and scale errors
constrain population summaries, latent correlations constrain item and annotator
ordering, and the computational thresholds screen unstable fits. Fixing the values
beforehand prevents us from choosing favorable cutoffs after seeing the fits, but
it does not make them disciplinary standards.

The baseline criteria have concrete scales. An intercept error of $.25$ is a quarter log-odds unit; around the generating intercept $-2.1$, shifts of that size move the zero-effect yes probability from about $.109$ to roughly $.087$ or $.136$. Relative scale errors of $.15$ and $.25$ permit deviations of $.24$ and $.40$ from the generating scale $1.6$. Correlation cutoffs assess preservation of latent ordering, with the stricter annotator cutoff reflecting the fact that only 12 annotator effects must be ranked. The $\widehat R$ and divergence rules screen the numerical fits rather than measurement validity. <!-- dqr-allow: algorithm-setting -->

The baseline thresholds are: median absolute intercept error at most $.25$; median absolute relative errors at most $.15$ for the item scale and $.25$ for the annotator scale; median correlations at least $.60$ for item effects, $.90$ for annotator effects, and $.65$ for conditional item probabilities; maximum key-parameter $\widehat R$ at most $1.05$; and no divergent transitions.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-uds-recovery

recovery_summary <- data.frame(
  quantity = c(
    "Median absolute intercept error",
    "Median absolute relative item-scale error",
    "Median absolute relative annotator-scale error",
    "Median item-effect correlation",
    "Median annotator-effect correlation",
    "Median item-probability correlation",
    "Largest key-parameter R-hat",
    "Divergent transitions"
  ),
  result = c(
    stats::median(abs(recovery$alpha_error)),
    stats::median(abs(recovery$sigma_item_relative_error)),
    stats::median(abs(recovery$sigma_annotator_relative_error)),
    stats::median(recovery$item_effect_correlation),
    stats::median(recovery$annotator_effect_correlation),
    stats::median(recovery$item_probability_correlation),
    max(recovery$maximum_key_rhat),
    sum(recovery$divergences)
  ),
  # Prespecified decision criteria, fixed before the released-data fit.
  threshold = c(0.25, 0.15, 0.25, 0.60, 0.90, 0.65, 1.05, 0) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
)

stopifnot(
  recovery_summary$result[[1]] <= recovery_summary$threshold[[1]],
  recovery_summary$result[[2]] <= recovery_summary$threshold[[2]],
  recovery_summary$result[[3]] <= recovery_summary$threshold[[3]],
  recovery_summary$result[[4]] >= recovery_summary$threshold[[4]],
  recovery_summary$result[[5]] >= recovery_summary$threshold[[5]],
  recovery_summary$result[[6]] >= recovery_summary$threshold[[6]],
  recovery_summary$result[[7]] <= recovery_summary$threshold[[7]],
  recovery_summary$result[[8]] == recovery_summary$threshold[[8]]
)

knitr::kable(recovery_summary, digits = 3)
```

To show how much the conclusion depends on those choices, we also apply a stricter sensitivity rule: maximum errors of $.20$, $.10$, and $.20$; minimum correlations of $.70$, $.95$, and $.75$; maximum $\widehat R$ of $1.01$; and zero divergences.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-uds-recovery-sensitivity

strict_threshold <- c(0.20, 0.10, 0.20, 0.70, 0.95, 0.75, 1.01, 0) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
direction <- c("at most", "at most", "at most", "at least",
               "at least", "at least", "at most", "equal to")
baseline_pass <- c(
  recovery_summary$result[1:3] <= recovery_summary$threshold[1:3],
  recovery_summary$result[4:6] >= recovery_summary$threshold[4:6],
  recovery_summary$result[[7]] <= recovery_summary$threshold[[7]],
  recovery_summary$result[[8]] == recovery_summary$threshold[[8]]
)
strict_pass <- c(
  recovery_summary$result[1:3] <= strict_threshold[1:3],
  recovery_summary$result[4:6] >= strict_threshold[4:6],
  recovery_summary$result[[7]] <= strict_threshold[[7]],
  recovery_summary$result[[8]] == strict_threshold[[8]]
)
recovery_sensitivity <- data.frame(
  quantity = recovery_summary$quantity,
  result = recovery_summary$result,
  direction = direction,
  baseline_threshold = recovery_summary$threshold,
  baseline_pass = baseline_pass,
  stricter_threshold = strict_threshold,
  stricter_pass = strict_pass
)
knitr::kable(recovery_sensitivity, digits = 3)
```

The baseline rule passes all eight criteria. Under the stricter rule, `r sum(strict_pass)` of eight pass. This comparison makes the decision sensitivity visible; it does not turn either threshold set into a scientific constant.

Medians can hide variation across only twelve simulations. The following interval
records the central 80% of the replicate-level diagnostics. It describes
[Monte Carlo](../statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd) variation across
these simulated fits. It is not a
[confidence interval](../statistical-inference/confidence-intervals.qmd) for
real-data performance.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-uds-recovery-variation

recovery_variation <- data.frame(
  quantity = c(
    "Absolute intercept error",
    "Absolute relative item-scale error",
    "Absolute relative annotator-scale error",
    "Item-effect correlation",
    "Annotator-effect correlation",
    "Item-probability correlation"
  ),
  lower_10 = vapply(
    list(
      abs(recovery$alpha_error),
      abs(recovery$sigma_item_relative_error),
      abs(recovery$sigma_annotator_relative_error),
      recovery$item_effect_correlation,
      recovery$annotator_effect_correlation,
      recovery$item_probability_correlation
    ),
    stats::quantile,
    numeric(1), probs = 0.10, names = FALSE
  ),
  upper_90 = vapply(
    list(
      abs(recovery$alpha_error),
      abs(recovery$sigma_item_relative_error),
      abs(recovery$sigma_annotator_relative_error),
      recovery$item_effect_correlation,
      recovery$annotator_effect_correlation,
      recovery$item_probability_correlation
    ),
    stats::quantile,
    numeric(1), probs = 0.90, names = FALSE
  )
)

knitr::kable(recovery_variation, digits = 3)
```

## Seeing variation across complete fits

```{r}
#| label: plot-uds-recovery
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Posterior medians from twelve complete recovery fits. Horizontal lines mark the generating values."

recovery_plot <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    replicate = recovery$replicate,
    quantity = "Population location",
    truth = generating_values[["alpha"]],
    estimate = recovery$alpha_estimate
  ),
  data.frame(
    replicate = recovery$replicate,
    quantity = "Item scale",
    truth = generating_values[["sigma_item"]],
    estimate = recovery$sigma_item_estimate
  ),
  data.frame(
    replicate = recovery$replicate,
    quantity = "Annotator scale",
    truth = generating_values[["sigma_annotator"]],
    estimate = recovery$sigma_annotator_estimate
  )
)

ggplot2::ggplot(
  recovery_plot,
  ggplot2::aes(replicate, estimate)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(
    data = unique(recovery_plot[c("quantity", "truth")]),
    ggplot2::aes(yintercept = truth),
    color = "grey65"
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(color = "steelblue4", alpha = 0.8, size = 2) + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ quantity, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1, 4, 8, 12) # dqr-allow: scale-boundary
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Recovery replicate", y = "Posterior median") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

The prespecified recovery criteria are met. With two or three responses per item, the fitted population distribution supplies substantial pooling, so recovery concerns aggregate regularized ordering. Precise lexical interpretation of every predicate node would require more item-specific information.

Successful recovery shows that the fitter can retrieve the declared targets when data arise from this model under this incidence design. It does not establish that real annotators follow the generator. The released-data analysis still requires posterior predictive checks and measurement limitations.

Twelve replicates can detect large failures, but they estimate tail behavior and pass rates imprecisely. Likewise, $\widehat R$ and divergences diagnose parts of Markov-chain computation, not measurement validity. Revisit [Markov chain Monte Carlo](../statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd) for the draw-based approximation and [checking Markov chains](../statistical-inference/checking-markov-chains.qmd) for convergence checks.

::: {.callout-note title="Check the recovery claim"}
1. Why is the observed incidence pattern held fixed?
2. Why must fitting occur inside every replicate?
3. Which recovery target is weakest in this design?
4. What does successful recovery fail to establish?

**Answers.** (1) Holding the incidence pattern fixed tests the information supplied by the actual sparse crossing rather than an easier balanced design. (2) Recovery evaluates the complete estimator, so every simulated response matrix must be fit anew. (3) The weakest target is the one with the lowest recorded recovery correlation or largest relative error, which the table makes explicit rather than naming from intuition. (4) Success does not show that the model generated the real annotations, that every item effect is precise, or that untested regimes would pass.
:::

## Recap

1. Recovery simulates known parameters under the released item--annotator incidence design and refits the whole model.
2. Absolute error, relative scale error, and latent-vector correlation answer different recovery questions.
3. The twelve completed fits evaluate the prespecified baseline regime; the additional stress regimes remain planned rather than evaluated.
4. MCMC diagnostics assess computation, while posterior predictive checks assess consequences of the fitted observation model.
5. The next page grounds agreement in the [Turkish PropBank measurement dossier](annotations-as-measurements.qmd#turkish-propbank-measurement-dossier) before fitting another crossed model.
